To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) the earth is flat; (b) the earth is round; and (c) the earth is not round, but it’s flat.

(1) significance thresholds are a major cause of the crisis of irreproducible research; (2) p-values are hardly replicable, and therefore not a reliable measure for replicability of a finding; (3) significance (p ≤.05) is not a reliable measure either; (4) significance thresholds lead to biased effect sizes, which in turn leads to wrong conclusions; and (5) removing significance thresholds is the only solution that addresses all of the above problems.

(1) p-values are not replicable, (2) the significance level of p ≤ 0.050 is not replicable either, (3) significance thresholds make cumulative knowledge unreliable, and (4) significance thresholds should be abandoned.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how we can best use statistics to make informed decisions about the practical relevance of scientific results.
the question of whether the widespread use of significance thresholds in research has contributed to making studies irreducible, or to make them seem irreducible.
the question how we can make research more reliable and more cumulative.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
p-values are neither a good nor a bad thing, but they can be used in a good way and in a bad way.
p > 0.001 is significant, p > 0.01 is suggestive, p >  0.05 is not significant, and p > 0 is not significant at all.
‘the earth is not flat’ (p < 0.001).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the earth is flat, but not because of p-values.
the earth is flat, and the crisis of reproducibility is not a crisis of reproduciblity.
the earth is flat (P > 0.5), but not because the earth is not round.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to move away from a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ decision based on significance, to a graded judgment of the strength of the evidence for a claim, based on the full statistical analysis of the data.
the crisis of irreproducible research is a consequence of a false belief in the power of significance tests.
the widespread use of significance thresholds has led to considerable distortion of scientific thinking and practice.
